OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 — DNS queries to known C&C domains AICommand & Control High
Flags DNS resolutions for the six SPECTRALVIPER C&C domains. Catches OceanLotus traffic earlier in the kill chain than IP-based detection (before the TCP connect) and survives attacker IP rotation as long as the domain stays alive. Rationale: Six C&C domains taken verbatim from the article body and Table 2; Table 2 explicitly maps four of them to SPECTRALVIPER infrastructure with their resolved IPs and first-seen dates (gatewayrvcenter.com → 139.180.128.42 etc.). DNS-based detection catches the malware before any IP rotation occurs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment or VirusTotal-style sandbox replaying domain lookups
  • Security researcher manually browsing the ESET IOCs to verify they resolve
  • Misconfigured DNS sinkhole still serving these names from a research zone
  • Recursive resolver caching a passive-DNS sweep from a partner tool
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msftewat.exe","MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","smartscreen.exe")
// suppress the EDR/AV's own reputation-lookup traffic
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the initiating process for the DNS query — was it a browser (likely user-driven), the EDR/TIP service (research), or an unsigned binary in %TEMP% / %APPDATA% (likely SPECTRALVIPER)? Step 2 (contain): sinkhole all six domains at the DNS resolver / DNS firewall; quarantine the device if the initiating process is anything other than a known TIP enrichment tool. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet via Defender DeviceFileEvents/DeviceProcessEvents — and pull NetFlow to the 8 OceanLotus C2 IPs for the same time window to spot devices that resolved successfully and connected.
let OceanLotusDomains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| extend Query = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).DnsQueryString)
| where Query has_any (OceanLotusDomains)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (OceanLotusDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, Query, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let OceanLotusDomains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (OceanLotusDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseName, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SPECTRALVIPER known-bad SHA1 — file write or execution on disk AIInstallation Medium
Hash-IOC match for any of the 20 SHA1s published by ESET as SPECTRALVIPER samples (both first-iteration and stable-version variants, plus FireAnt supply-chain stage-one droppers). Highest-fidelity signal in this article. Rationale: Twenty SHA1 hashes from the ESET IOC bundle covering both campaigns (FireAnt supply-chain stage-one droppers + SPECTRALVIPER backdoor — first-iteration and stable variants per Table 1). Hash matches are zero-FP unless an analyst is intentionally analyzing the sample. We hit both process-execution and file-write tables to catch dropper-on-disk before execution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst manually detonating the sample in a sandbox VM enrolled in production EDR
  • Threat-intel team downloading the hashes from VT for IOC verification
  • Backup/imaging restore process replaying an archived infected disk
  • Defender ATP's own Sample Submission round-tripping the binary
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","smartscreen.exe","MsMpEngCP.exe")
// suppress AV's own sample handling
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): immediately pivot on DeviceId — pull all DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents for the past 90 days; confirm whether the file ran (DeviceProcessEvents) or only landed (DeviceFileEvents only). Step 2 (contain): EDR-isolate the host; force a full Defender scan; capture the binary for offline analysis; block all 20 SHA1s + the eight C2 IPs at the perimeter. Step 3 (hunt): retro-scan the entire fleet for any of these SHA1s back to Jan 2024 (campaign start was mid-2024); pull DeviceNetworkEvents to the C2 IPs/domains in UC1/UC2 for the same hosts; query DeviceImageLoadEvents for any DLLs sharing a parent folder with matched samples to find side-loading hosts.
let SpectralViperSHA1 = dynamic(["D511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39F","59A8553A4F8130F576AB234E0B220BE4D4DA0E98","9CA1A5C7F79882DB913534C1E62B26BCDCB9F6DD","A8E2BBBFCB86500322D2367744FA12755AB0C165","F74F1FEB62B662CDA489FDB2453727824E55ACB9","F8F8209987CA7F139DE6A62F9E6EE21BD2AE93A9","19A69F856EFA811C376F68E4FEB0997B4724F8BD","490194E9BB5128ECA8693AD9E610891C2ED185AF","51176139B0B2220B802C1578A4994DF68DF5BCD1","91F042F59BE4BDCB6E5EA21B91DECD731C175B54","A177ED0BFFEB1EFE1D9D31D72A82EF2625AE646D","B7B2D2DB544F9EEA74453CDF2B8BEEA58CF07C48","4AD36AD6C165B5174967020CB1A3358F78D7A283","57352B3CEEE32216E5AA20BAA848483D7AB5A6FB","9BC06DF9F932746A05EE728C8B103BD3BA6BF395","865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D","41CB8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B0","0037DBB0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D20","5D6194BB48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918B","B028E947150764A71DEEF498DE6F8C95ECCCB445"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | where SHA1 in (SpectralViperSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (SpectralViperSHA1)
    | project Timestamp, EventTable="DeviceProcessEvents", DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA1, AccountName),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | where SHA1 in (SpectralViperSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (SpectralViperSHA1)
    | project Timestamp, EventTable="DeviceFileEvents", DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine="",
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessSHA1, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
let SpectralViperSHA1 = dynamic(["D511B77459673EC42163F19E300FF1D233B6C39F","59A8553A4F8130F576AB234E0B220BE4D4DA0E98","9CA1A5C7F79882DB913534C1E62B26BCDCB9F6DD","A8E2BBBFCB86500322D2367744FA12755AB0C165","F74F1FEB62B662CDA489FDB2453727824E55ACB9","F8F8209987CA7F139DE6A62F9E6EE21BD2AE93A9","19A69F856EFA811C376F68E4FEB0997B4724F8BD","490194E9BB5128ECA8693AD9E610891C2ED185AF","51176139B0B2220B802C1578A4994DF68DF5BCD1","91F042F59BE4BDCB6E5EA21B91DECD731C175B54","A177ED0BFFEB1EFE1D9D31D72A82EF2625AE646D","B7B2D2DB544F9EEA74453CDF2B8BEEA58CF07C48","4AD36AD6C165B5174967020CB1A3358F78D7A283","57352B3CEEE32216E5AA20BAA848483D7AB5A6FB","9BC06DF9F932746A05EE728C8B103BD3BA6BF395","865A1739337D3303B3AB02C5E694C22B79C42B7D","41CB8CD78B8DB76563E4F972ABE817CEEE9CF9B0","0037DBB0FEA981D02F6F76DE81EBAEFCB68B7D20","5D6194BB48FEBB91A10D1462461A012FAFC0918B","B028E947150764A71DEEF498DE6F8C95ECCCB445"]);
union
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
    | where SHA1 in (SpectralViperSHA1)
    | project TimeGenerated, EventTable="ImProcessCreate", DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1, ActorUsername),
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
    | where TargetFileSHA1 in (SpectralViperSHA1)
    | project TimeGenerated, EventTable="ImFileEvent", DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1=TargetFileSHA1, ActorUsername)

FireAnt Metakit supply-chain — malicious update spawning suspicious child AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the FireAnt Metakit supply-chain campaign (Oct 2025 → Mar 2026) where the legitimate Vietnamese stock-platform updater was hijacked to deliver SPECTRALVIPER. Flags any FireAnt-process tree where the legitimate trading binary spawns living-off-the-land binaries or writes/executes content from %TEMP% / %APPDATA% — neither of which a normal market-data app does. Rationale: FireAnt Metakit is the named victim platform in the article's supply-chain campaign — a Vietnamese stock-trading application. A legit trading app spawning PowerShell, mshta, rundll32 or writing to %TEMP% is anomalous regardless of region. Pattern lifted from `pattern-process-tree` (parent narrows scope, child narrows behaviour). Hunting tier because the parent-process name may vary across versions and child set is broad. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FireAnt installer / auto-updater calling cmd.exe to register file associations on first launch
  • FireAnt support staff running diagnostic PowerShell scripts inside the install directory
  • Endpoint protection scanning unpacked FireAnt update files in %TEMP% during install
  • Windows installer service relaunch under a fresh logon session creating a child cmd.exe shim
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("installer","/uninstall","vcredist","setup")
  and not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/c \"reg add")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — legitimate FireAnt update logic shouldn't include `IEX`, `DownloadString`, `-EncodedCommand`, certutil `-decode`, or rundll32 of a DLL outside `%ProgramFiles%`. Pull the InitiatingProcessSHA1 and check it against the 20 SPECTRALVIPER hashes. Step 2 (contain): if cmdline looks malicious, isolate the host and block the FireAnt updater SHA1 in EDR; preserve the on-disk FireAnt installer for hash submission. Step 3 (hunt): query for the same parent SHA1 across all FireAnt users in the org to identify breadth of exposure; check DeviceNetworkEvents for the host hitting any of the eight OceanLotus C2 IPs in the 24h after install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\FireAnt\\","\\Metakit\\","\\FireAnt Metakit\\")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe")
   or FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA1,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("FireAnt","Metakit")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wmic.exe")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender) @ParentImage:(*\\FireAnt*.exe OR *\\fireant*.exe OR *\\Metakit*.exe OR *\\metakit*.exe) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\curl.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/(fireant|metakit)/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|certutil|bitsadmin|curl|wmic)\.exe$/i OR regex("\\\\(Temp|AppData\\\\Roaming|ProgramData|Users\\\\Public)\\\\", field=ImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="FireAnt*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\FireAnt*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\Metakit*") (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe") OR Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Temp\\*","*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*","*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*","*\\ProgramData\\*\\Temp\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_sha1
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="FireAnt*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\FireAnt*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\Metakit*") (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe") OR Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Temp\\*","*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\*","*\\AppData\\Roaming\\*","*\\ProgramData\\*\\Temp\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_sha1
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
OceanLotus historical C2 — DNS tunneling to unusually long subdomain (Denis/SOUNDBITE) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Denis/SOUNDBITE family's DNS-tunneling protocol — OceanLotus's known legacy C2 channel that the article calls out as part of their continuing toolkit. Flags high-entropy / unusually long subdomains queried by non-browser processes, scoped to second-level domains seen in OceanLotus campaigns. Catches new C&C domains that aren't yet on the indicator list. Rationale: Article names Denis (aka SOUNDBITE) as OceanLotus's signature DNS-tunneling backdoor still in their arsenal. DNS-tunneling detection works regardless of the specific C&C domain (catches infrastructure not yet IOC'd). 30-char subdomain + 20+ distinct subdomains per SLD is the standard tunneling-channel shape; excluding browsers cuts the major FP source (Chrome remote-debug telemetry, ESNI, etc.). Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/oceanlotus-external-espionage-domestic-targeting/ • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0099/
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DNSSEC validation chasing CDS / DS records with long Base32-encoded labels
  • Antivirus / EDR cloud-reputation lookups using long hash-prefix subdomains (e.g. Microsoft SmartScreen, McAfee GTI)
  • Email anti-spam services querying long DKIM/SPF lookup keys
  • Backup / observability agents using DNS for cloud-bucket pointers (some S3 setups query *.s3.amazonaws.com via long encoded subdomains)
  • Microsoft Office click-to-run telemetry occasionally emits long subdomain probes
Suppression filter
| where SLD !endswith ".trustwave.com" and SLD !endswith ".symantec.com" and SLD !endswith ".mcafee.com"
  and SLD !endswith ".mcafeegti.com" and SLD !endswith ".sophosxl.net" and SLD !endswith ".webrootcloudav.com"
  and SLD !endswith ".smartscreen.microsoft.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): on a flagged DeviceId, pull the initiating process — is it a known browser plugin / endpoint-agent / mail-gateway, or is it an unsigned binary in user-writable space (likely Denis)? Step 2 (contain): if the initiating binary is unknown, EDR-isolate; capture the binary and pivot to SHA1 against the 20 known SPECTRALVIPER hashes; sinkhole the SLD at DNS firewall. Step 3 (hunt): correlate the same DeviceId for outbound connections to the eight known OceanLotus C2 IPs; query the same SLD across the fleet for other affected hosts; review the binary's persistence footprint (DeviceRegistryEvents on Run/RunOnce keys, scheduled tasks).
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| extend Query = tolower(tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).DnsQueryString))
| where isnotempty(Query)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","safari.exe","opera.exe")
| extend Subdomain = tostring(split(Query, ".")[0])
| extend SubLen = strlen(Subdomain)
| extend SLD = strcat(tostring(split(Query, ".")[-2]), ".", tostring(split(Query, ".")[-1]))
| where SubLen >= 30
| summarize DistinctSubs = dcount(Subdomain), QueryCount = count(),
            SampleQuery = any(Query), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SLD
| where DistinctSubs >= 20 and QueryCount >= 50
| order by DistinctSubs desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQueryTypeName in~ ("A","AAAA","TXT","NULL")
| extend Subdomain = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[0])
| extend SubLen = strlen(Subdomain)
| extend SLD = strcat(tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[-2]), ".", tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[-1]))
| where SubLen >= 30
| summarize DistinctSubs = dcount(Subdomain), QueryCount = count(),
            SampleQuery = any(DnsQuery), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, SLD
| where DistinctSubs >= 20 and QueryCount >= 50
| order by DistinctSubs desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR cisco.umbrella OR linux.auditd) @dns.question.name:????????????????????????????????* -@process.name:(chrome.exe OR msedge.exe OR firefox.exe OR Chrome.exe OR MsEdge.exe OR Firefox.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera)\.exe$/i
| Subdomain := splitString(field=DomainName, by=".", index=0)
| SubLen := length(Subdomain)
| SubLen >= 30
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function={ DistinctSubs := count(field=Subdomain, distinct=true) | QueryCount := count() })
| DistinctSubs >= 20
| QueryCount >= 50
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.message_type="QUERY" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.record_type _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| rex field=query "^(?<sub>[^.]+)\.(?<sld>[^.]+\.[^.]+)$"
| eval sub_len = len(sub)
| where sub_len >= 30 AND record_type IN ("A","AAAA","TXT","NULL")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime dc(sub) as distinct_subs by src sld
| where distinct_subs > 20 AND count > 50
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - distinct_subs
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.message_type="QUERY" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.record_type _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| rex field=query "^(?<sub>[^.]+)\.(?<sld>[^.]+\.[^.]+)$"

| where distinct_subs > 20 AND count > 50

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("139.162.11.152", "142.91.98.77", "139.180.128.42", "139.99.33.239", "166.88.77.186", "103.119.47.104", "38.60.245.37", "194.68.26.241") or RemoteUrl has_any ("financemachinelearning.com", "gatewayrvcenter.com", "coachcybersecurity.com", "mxprodesign.com", "power-sync-services.com", "leadingfilipinoteams.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["139.162.11.152", "142.91.98.77", "139.180.128.42", "139.99.33.239", "166.88.77.186", "103.119.47.104", "38.60.245.37", "194.68.26.241"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com", "gatewayrvcenter.com", "coachcybersecurity.com", "mxprodesign.com", "power-sync-services.com", "leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("139.162.11.152", "142.91.98.77", "139.180.128.42", "139.99.33.239", "166.88.77.186", "103.119.47.104", "38.60.245.37", "194.68.26.241")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries Command & Control Medium
Long subdomain labels + frequent queries to a single 2LD = DNS C2/exfil.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1048.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemotePort == 53 and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend qlen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where qlen > 50
| extend SecondLevelDomain = extract(@"([\w-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,})$", 1, RemoteUrl)
| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20
| order by qcount desc
// ASIM ImDnsActivity normalises Windows DNS, Sysmon EID 22, Linux dnsmasq, etc.
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DnsQueryTypeName == "TXT"
| summarize Queries = count(), DistinctNames = dcount(DnsQuery)
            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Queries > 200    // tune to TXT-query baseline for environment
| order by Queries desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
    where DNS.message_type="QUERY"
    by DNS.src, DNS.query
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| eval qlen=len(query)
| where qlen > 50
| rex field=query "(?<second_level_domain>[\w-]+\.[\w-]+)$"
| stats sum(count) AS qcount, dc(query) AS unique_subs, max(qlen) AS max_label
    by src, second_level_domain
| where qcount > 100 AND unique_subs > 20
| sort - qcount
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

GitHub to Disable npm Install Scripts by Default to Stop Supply Chain Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

GitHub has announced what it said are "breaking changes" coming to npm version 12, one of which turns off install scripts by default to combat software supply chain threats. The changes aim to combat attack techniques that abuse the "npm install" command to trigger the execution of malicious code using npm lifecycle hooks. "Npm install" is used to download and install all the necessary

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] npm install with --allow-git / --allow-remote / --allow-scripts bypass flag · [LLM] npm install with --ignore-scripts=false or NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS override
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm install pointing at non-default registry via --registry or config · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GitHub to Disable npm Install Scripts by Default to Stop Supply Chain Attacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm install lifecycle script spawns interpreter or network-fetcher child
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] npm publish / login / auth-token write from a developer endpoint · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
npm install lifecycle script spawns interpreter or network-fetcher child AIInstallation Medium
Detects suspicious interpreter or downloader children of npm.exe / node.exe during package install — the exact lifecycle-script code-execution surface GitHub is disabling by default in npm 12. The article specifically names preinstall, install, and postinstall scripts (plus implicit node-gyp rebuilds) as the abuse vector. Rationale: Article names preinstall/install/postinstall lifecycle scripts and implicit node-gyp rebuild as the largest npm code-execution surface. Parent-process pivot (npm/node) plus interpreter/downloader child is the canonical shape of recent npm supply-chain payloads (e.g. recent Microsoft GitHub repo worm). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://github.blog/changelog/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native-addon builds where postinstall invokes node-gyp which shells out to cmd.exe and python
  • Developer-owned packages whose preinstall scripts legitimately curl down a binary asset (e.g. puppeteer Chromium, esbuild prebuilt)
  • CI runners where npm install routinely spawns powershell/bash wrappers for cross-platform scripts
  • electron-builder / node-pre-gyp pulling prebuilt binaries on first install
  • Yarn/pnpm wrappers re-invoking npm under the hood and chaining shell calls
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp" and ChildImage endswith "\\cmd.exe" and ChildCmd has_any ("python","msbuild")) | where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("puppeteer","playwright","esbuild","node-pre-gyp","electron") and ChildCmd has_any ("https://","download"))

1) Triage: pull the full process tree and InitiatingProcessCommandLine; identify the package being installed by checking CWD for package.json/package-lock.json and which dependency owns the running install hook (npm logs at %APPDATA%\npm-cache\_logs). 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke any npm/GitHub auth tokens present on it (npm token list, gh auth status), and freeze CI runners that share the registry. 3) Hunt: pivot on the package name + version across the fleet, query for the same parent->child shape in the last 30 days, check npm registry advisories and ThreatFox for that package, and inspect ~/.npmrc and project .npmrc for unexpected registry or authToken entries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","npm i ","npm rebuild","node-gyp rebuild")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or CommandLine has_any ("npm install","npm ci","npm rebuild","node-gyp rebuild")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm install with --allow-git / --allow-remote / --allow-scripts bypass flag AIWeaponization High
Detects explicit use of the new npm 12 allow-list flags (--allow-git, --allow-remote, --allow-scripts) or .npmrc allowScripts=true, which re-open the very code-execution paths GitHub is closing by default. After upgrade, routine use of these flags on developer endpoints is an adversary tell. Rationale: Article calls out --allow-git as the post-v12 opt-in for Git dependencies and --allow-remote for remote URL tarballs, plus the explicit allowScripts default flip. Article also notes the .npmrc-overrides-Git-executable bypass — these flags are the literal strings to grep for. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A senior dev who explicitly trusts and runs a Git dependency with --allow-git for one-off prototyping
  • Internal monorepo tooling that legitimately needs --allow-remote for an internal-only tarball mirror
  • CI pipelines that intentionally set allowScripts=true for native-addon builds (e.g. binding.gyp packages)
  • Vendor build steps invoked by Yarn/pnpm that pass the flags through to nested npm calls
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\actions-runner\\","\\agent\\","\\TeamCity\\","\\Jenkins\\","\\gitlab-runner\\") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the package and registry being installed - check the CWD, package.json, and any --registry argument on the same command line. Pull npm-cli logs from %APPDATA%\npm-cache\_logs. 2) Contain: if the package is from a public/unknown registry, isolate the host and block the registry FQDN at egress; freeze any artifact built by this run. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same package name + version with these flags; look for follow-on outbound connections from node.exe / npm.exe to non-corporate IPs within 10 minutes; check .npmrc files org-wide for allowScripts=true or registry overrides.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--allow-git","--allow-remote","--allow-scripts","allowScripts=true","allowScripts = true")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--allow-git","--allow-remote","--allow-scripts","allowScripts=true","allowScripts = true")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm install pointing at non-default registry via --registry or config AIDelivery Medium
Hunts npm/node invocations that point at a registry other than npmjs.org or known mirrors — the canonical dependency-confusion / typosquatting setup, and the path an attacker uses once they have a foothold to redirect a developer to a malicious mirror. Pairs with the v12 install-script hardening: an attacker losing scripts will pivot to redirecting the registry itself. Rationale: Article frames npm install as the supply-chain entry point and v12 closes the script-execution path; redirecting the registry is the natural pivot left to attackers. Non-default --registry is a textbook dependency-confusion precursor and is high-signal on developer endpoints (org-approved registries are usually known). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1584.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers using an internal Verdaccio / Artifactory / Nexus / GitHub Packages mirror
  • Open-source contributors pointing at a forked registry for testing a new feature
  • CI runners configured with a corporate mirror that fronts npmjs.org
  • One-off install from a vendor-provided registry during a POC
  • Yarn invocations that pass --registry through to nested npm calls
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("verdaccio","artifactory","nexus","npm.pkg.github.com","jfrog","myget") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\actions-runner\\","\\Jenkins\\","\\TeamCity\\","\\agent\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the registry URL from the command line and resolve it - check WHOIS, certificate transparency, and the org's approved-mirror list. Look at the package(s) being installed in the same command. 2) Contain: if the registry is not on the approved list, isolate the host and block the FQDN at egress; quarantine any node_modules built during this run. 3) Hunt: pivot on the registry FQDN across DeviceNetworkEvents for the last 30 days; check whether other developers / CI runners hit the same URL; query for follow-on outbound connections from node.exe within 5 minutes of the install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--registry" or ProcessCommandLine has "config set registry"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "registry.npmjs.org"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "registry.yarnpkg.com"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "registry.npmmirror.com"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has "--registry" or CommandLine has "config set registry"
| where CommandLine !has "registry.npmjs.org"
| where CommandLine !has "registry.yarnpkg.com"
| where CommandLine !has "registry.npmmirror.com"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm publish / login / auth-token write from a developer endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces npm auth and publish CLI activity plus .npmrc credential-file writes on workstations - the precursor to a package-hijack supply-chain attack. Splits the original (broken) single-column lookup into a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents so neither query references a non-canonical column. Rationale: Article frames npm install as the supply-chain risk, but credential write + publish from a developer endpoint is how a package gets hijacked at source. Hunts for npm publish/login/token CLI flows and .npmrc credential-file writes (which carry _authToken=). Uses canonical Defender columns only - replaces the previous query that referenced a non-existent NpmrcWrites column with a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/npmrc
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal package authors running npm publish to a private registry as part of normal workflow
  • Onboarding flows that create ~/.npmrc with corporate registry tokens
  • CI agents publishing release artifacts on tag push
  • Developers running npm whoami / npm login after rotating their npm token
  • IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains) writing project-local .npmrc files
Suppression filter
| where not (Initiator has_any ("actions-runner","gitlab-runner","TeamCity","Jenkins","agent.exe") and EventKind == "npm_auth_cli")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user is an authorized package publisher; for .npmrc writes, read the file and look for _authToken=, registry overrides, or always-auth=true on non-corporate hosts. 2) Contain: if unauthorized publish, immediately revoke the npm token (npm token revoke) and the user's npmjs.com session; if a malicious package version was published, contact npm security to deprecate/unpublish and notify downstream consumers. 3) Hunt: pivot on the username across npm registry audit logs for prior publishes; check whether the same .npmrc token appears on other endpoints; look for outbound POSTs to registry.npmjs.org/_token or /-/v1/login from the same host in the last 24h.
let NpmAuth = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=ProcessCommandLine, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
let NpmrcChange = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=strcat(FolderPath,"\\",FileName), Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
NpmAuth
| union NpmrcChange
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=CommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=TargetFilePath)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @CommandLine:(*"npm publish"* OR *"npm login"* OR *"npm adduser"* OR *"npm token create"* OR *"npm token revoke"*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.NPMRC))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/^.*\\(npm(\.exe|\.cmd)?|node\.exe)$/i
| regex("(npm\\s+(publish|login|adduser|whoami)|npm\\s+token\\s+(create|revoke))", field=CommandLine)) OR (#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\.npmrc$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, TargetFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(npm\s+publish|npm\s+login|npm\s+adduser|npm\s+token\s+(create|revoke)|npm\s+whoami)") | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name=".npmrc" AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
npm install with --ignore-scripts=false or NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS override AIWeaponization High
Catches explicit attempts to re-enable lifecycle scripts that npm 12 disables by default - via --ignore-scripts=false CLI flag, NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false env var, or the new approve-scripts opt-in path. After the v12 upgrade rolls out, an adversary with code-exec on a developer box needs to flip this back on to land lifecycle-based persistence. Rationale: Article explicitly names --ignore-scripts as the flag npm 12's new default replaces, and references npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as the opt-in. NPM_CONFIG_* envvar form is documented npm config behavior. After the v12 ramp, any of these strings on a developer endpoint is an adversary opting out of the new default. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/config
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes

  • Build scripts that legitimately set NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false for native-module builds
  • Dockerfile RUN lines that force --foreground-scripts for log visibility
  • Internal tooling that wraps npm and passes the flag through transparently
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "allow-scripts-pending" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName endswith "\\explorer.exe" and AccountName has_any ("dev","engineer","build"))

1) Triage: confirm the user, package set, and whether this was the documented upgrade-prep approve-scripts flow vs a fresh install with the flag flipped. Pull surrounding child processes within +/- 60s. 2) Contain: if not approved, isolate the host and capture node_modules for the project; revoke any tokens present in .npmrc. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same flag pattern in the last 30 days, look for the same flag combined with --registry pointing off-mainstream, and check whether the same user/host hit UC1 (lifecycle-script suspicious child) in the same window.

| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Baileys messages.upsert with requestId field — exploitation marker (CVE-2026-48063) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-48063 in Baileys (WhatsApp Web library) by hunting for the application-log signature documented in the advisory's workaround section: a messages.upsert event carrying a requestId field. The advisory tells defenders to drop exactly these events as the only practical mitigation, so their presence on a vulnerable build is a direct exploitation marker. Rationale: Advisory 'Workarounds' section explicitly names dropping messages.upsert events that contain a requestId field as the only real workaround — making that exact field combination the highest-fidelity exploitation signature the article gives us. Cross-referenced patch commit 3beb08ee and the GHSA advisory page. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
ATT&CKT1566.003 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Already-patched Baileys (>=7.0.0-rc12 / >=6.7.22) still emitting a benign requestId on legitimate placeholderResendMessage flows during normal history recovery
  • Custom Baileys forks that legitimately use requestId for in-house tracing/observability tagging
  • QA / staging debug logs where placeholderResendMessage is intentionally fuzzed to test resilience
  • Alternative WA libraries (whatsapp-web.js, venom-bot) emitting the substring 'messages.upsert' in their own log shape without the Baileys vuln
Suppression filter
| where not(SyslogMessage has_any ("version=7.0.0-rc12", "version=7.0.0-rc13", "version=6.7.22", "version=6.7.23"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the Baileys version on the alerting host (npm ls baileys / cat node_modules/baileys/package.json). If <7.0.0-rc12 or <6.7.22, treat the requestId-bearing upsert as an exploitation attempt; capture the SyslogMessage and the offending requestId for IR. Step 2 — Contain: terminate the Node.js process owning the WA socket and revoke the linked-device session inside the WhatsApp mobile app — this invalidates the attacker's spoofing channel and forces re-pair. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate every host running the vulnerable npm package; pivot on the requestId pattern across 30 days of forwarded app logs to find earlier silent spoofing that the upsert handler accepted.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessId, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has_any ("node", "nodejs", "pm2") or SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert" and SyslogMessage has "requestId"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") AND "messages.upsert" AND requestId
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName="*node.exe" OR ImageFileName="*/node")
| regex("baileys|whiskeysockets", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, UserName], function=count())

Baileys app state sync corruption — repeated reconciliation failures from a single peer AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the second documented impact of CVE-2026-48063: 'corrupt the app state sync system by sending fake key shares'. Hunts for clusters of app-state-sync validation errors, key-share rejections, or sync rollbacks emitted by Baileys-based Node.js services within a short window — the cascading-correction pattern the advisory describes. Rationale: Advisory Impact paragraph explicitly cites 'corrupt the app state sync system by sending fake key shares' and 'no workarounds for the app state sync jamming' — making clusters of app-state-sync failures the natural detectable signature of the second exploit path. Anchor strings (appStateSync, AppStateSyncKey, fetchAppStateSyncKey) come from the public Baileys source tree referenced by patch commit 3beb08ee. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Network instability causing transient WA socket disconnects and benign appStateSync retries
  • Legitimate bulk-message flows that trigger normal sync reconciliation
  • Account using multiple linked devices simultaneously, producing concurrent appStateSync deltas
  • Baileys upgrade in progress where a new key-share format temporarily mismatches cached state
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the host runs a vulnerable Baileys version (<7.0.0-rc12 / <6.7.22). If yes and >=3 appStateSync failures occurred in <10 min from the same session, treat as exploitation. Step 2 — Contain: stop the affected Node.js service, wipe the local Baileys auth/keys directory, and re-pair via QR / 8-digit code from the mobile device. Do NOT restore from snapshot — local state may already be corrupted. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the WA session ID / Baileys auth folder across all other hosts using shared credentials; check for messages.upsert + requestId hits (UC1) on the same time window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| summarize ProcessStarts = count(), FirstStart = min(Timestamp), LastStart = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ProcessStarts >= 3
| order by LastStart desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("baileys", "@whiskeysockets/baileys")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("appStateSync", "AppStateSyncKey", "app-state-sync", "syncAppState", "fetchAppStateSyncKey")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("fail", "error", "invalid", "rollback", "reject", "mismatch", "timeout")
| summarize FailCount = count(), SampleMessage = any(SyslogMessage) by Computer, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FailCount >= 3
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") AND (appStateSync OR AppStateSyncKey OR fetchAppStateSyncKey OR syncAppState) AND (fail OR error OR invalid OR rollback OR reject OR mismatch)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ImageFileName="*node.exe" OR ImageFileName="*/node")
| regex("baileys|whiskeysockets", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName], function=count(as=launches))
| launches > 5
APPLICATION
index=app OR index=nodejs OR index=application (baileys OR "@whiskeysockets/baileys") ("appStateSync" OR "AppStateSyncKey" OR "app-state-sync" OR "syncAppState" OR "fetchAppStateSyncKey") ("fail" OR "error" OR "invalid" OR "rollback" OR "reject" OR "mismatch" OR "timeout")
| bin _time span=10m as bucket
| stats count as fail_count values(source) as sources by host process bucket
| where fail_count >= 3
| sort - bucket
Vulnerable Baileys npm package presence (<7.0.0-rc12 / <6.7.22) — fleet inventory hunt AIWeaponization High
Identifies hosts with a vulnerable Baileys install on disk so the SOC can drive patch adoption for CVE-2026-48063. Pivots on node_modules/baileys and node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys package.json writes captured by EDR file telemetry. Escalates internet-facing services that remain unpatched >7 days post-advisory. Rationale: Article specifies the exact vulnerable npm package names (baileys, @whiskeysockets/baileys) and the version cut-offs (<7.0.0-rc12, <6.7.22). The file-event signature on node_modules/<pkg>/package.json is the most reliable cross-EDR fingerprint of installation regardless of host OS. Cross-checked the GHSA advisory and the npm registry pages. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://www.npmjs.com/package/baileys • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@whiskeysockets/baileys
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Already-patched installs (>=7.0.0-rc12 / >=6.7.22) — file presence alone doesn't reveal version; analyst must read package.json contents
  • Developer workstations with the package installed for local testing (lower severity than production hosts)
  • Containers built FROM a vulnerable layer but never run in production
  • Old node_modules trees inside a backup snapshot mounted on a sandbox host
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: for every alerting host, read node_modules/baileys/package.json (or @whiskeysockets variant) and extract the version field. Hosts on >=7.0.0-rc12 or >=6.7.22 are patched — close. Otherwise continue. Step 2 — Contain: prioritise internet-facing or production WA-bot services; schedule package upgrade via npm install baileys@^7.0.0-rc12 (or 6.7.22 for the v6 line) and redeploy. Step 3 — Hunt: cross-reference against UC1 (messages.upsert + requestId) and UC2 (appStateSync failures) on the same hosts to confirm whether exploitation already occurred before the patch lands.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "node_modules" and FolderPath has "baileys"
| where FileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Writers = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5) by DeviceName, FolderPath
| where LastSeen > ago(7d)
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules" and TargetFilePath has "baileys"
| where TargetFileName =~ "package.json"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath
| where LastSeen > ago(7d)
| order by LastSeen desc
