Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Web-facing exposure of dev.env / .env config file (returns 200) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts HTTP requests to dev.env / .env / .env.* paths that returned a 2xx response, indicating a misconfigured web server is leaking the very file that ships AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random. CVE-2026-48031 weaponises exactly this file, so any successful retrieval is a direct precursor to JWT forgery. Rationale: Targets the exact filename (dev.env) named at line 10 of the advisory plus common .env variants the same template is renamed to. 2xx/3xx status confirms the leak actually happened. Cross-checked CVE-2026-48031 advisory and dhax/go-base PR #31. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal CI/CD pipeline pulling .env from a private artifact server
  • DAST/SAST scanners (Burp, ZAP, Nessus) probing for exposed dotfiles
  • Penetration testers running ffuf / dirsearch with default wordlists
  • Internal developer documentation site serving a sanitized .env.example
  • Cloud config-management agents (Consul, etcd) syncing env templates over HTTP
Suppression filter
and csUserAgent !has_any ("Burp","OWASP ZAP","Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","ffuf","dirsearch","gobuster") and cIP !in (KnownScannerIPs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on cIP/sourceIPAddress; was the request from a known scanner, a developer subnet, or external? Inspect User-Agent and response size — non-empty 200 on dev.env is critical. 2) Contain: rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET immediately to a 32+ byte random value, invalidate all outstanding JWT/refresh tokens, and add a WebACL/NGINX deny for .env/dev.env paths. Take the affected service off the perimeter if the secret was leaked externally. 3) Hunt: look for forged-token use — admin API calls from the same source IP within 24h, /api/v1/token/refresh hits with unknown sub claims, and any new sessions whose iat predates the secret rotation. Sweep all Go services for github.com/dhax/go-base in go.mod.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/dev.env","/.env","/.env.dev","/.env.local","/.env.development")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe","goland64.exe","idea64.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
// IIS-fronted Go service exposure
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)$"
| where scStatus in (200,206,301,302)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| union (
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DeviceProduct in ("WAF","Application Gateway","CloudFront","NGINX","Apache")
    | where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(^|/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)(\?|$)"
    | where toint(EventOutcome) between (200 .. 399)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, sSiteName=DestinationHostName, cIP=SourceIP, csMethod=RequestMethod, csUriStem=RequestURL, csUriQuery="", scStatus=toint(EventOutcome), csUserAgent=RequestClientApplication
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web exposure of dev.env / .env config file
id: 7c1a4b3e-2f57-4c61-9c4e-3a1e2f8b5d11
description: Detects HTTP requests retrieving dev.env or .env files that may leak the hardcoded AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random used by github.com/dhax/go-base (CVE-2026-48031).
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
  - https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:

detection:

      - 301
      - 302

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ConnectionDirection=1
| (RemotePort=80 OR RemotePort=443 OR RemotePort=3000 OR RemotePort=8080)
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest | DomainName=/.*/ }, field=[aid], include=[DomainName])
| regex("/(dev\.env|\.env)(\.[a-z]+)?($|\?)", field=CommandLine, strict=false)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())

fields @timestamp, eventName, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn, requestParameters.bucketName, requestParameters.key, errorCode
| filter eventSource = "s3.amazonaws.com"
      and eventName in ["GetObject", "GetObjectAcl"]
      and (requestParameters.key like /(?i)(^|\/)(dev\.env|\.env(\.[a-z]+)?)$/)
      and not isPresent(errorCode)
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

github.com/dhax/go-base supply-chain footprint in go.mod / build artifacts AIReconnaissance High
Identifies hosts (developer laptops, CI runners, container build agents) where go.mod, go.sum, vendor/modules.txt or Dockerfiles reference github.com/dhax/go-base. The advisory states 'all versions before commit cc82b974...' are vulnerable, so footprinting the dependency is the first step before patching can begin. Rationale: Anchors on the exact module path github.com/dhax/go-base named in the advisory's Affected Component list. go.mod / go.sum / Dockerfile additions and `go build`/`go mod` invocations that reference the module pin the asset surface that needs patching to the cc82b974... commit. Cross-checked CVE-2026-48031 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/commits/master
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1518
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer evaluating the boilerplate for a new microservice
  • Security team running SCA scan that already covers this CVE
  • CI job intentionally pinning to the patched commit (>= cc82b9740fa6)
  • Internal fork of go-base that is already patched
  • Vulnerability scanner (Trivy, Grype, Snyk) reading go.sum files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("trivy.exe","grype.exe","snyk.exe","syft.exe") and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every host/build agent that touched go.mod referencing dhax/go-base in the last 30d. For each, pull the pinned version (the @ pseudo-version after the path). Anything before commit cc82b9740fa6 (2026-05-17) is vulnerable. 2) Contain: file Jira/Linear tickets to bump the dependency past cc82b9740fa6, regenerate AUTH_JWT_SECRET (>=32 chars), and force a token revocation on next deploy. Block new builds on the unpatched version via a renovate/dependabot policy. 3) Hunt: identify all running services derived from the vulnerable code — query container registries for images whose go.mod includes the unpatched pin. For any that were ever internet-facing, run the JWT-forgery UC against their access logs back to the deploy date.

)

Admin / privileged API call without a preceding SUCCESSFUL login (JWT forgery indicator) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Forged tokens signed with the hardcoded 'random' secret never traverse the application's login or refresh flows — they appear as bearer-auth-only requests. This UC pivots web access logs for /api/v1/admin/* and /api/v1/me hits whose source IP has no /api/v1/login/* 2xx in the prior 24h, the behavioural signature of token forgery. Rationale: The advisory's PoC explicitly hits /api/v1/admin/users, /api/v1/me, and /api/v1/token/refresh with a forged Bearer token (no login step). Modelling 'admin hit without a recent successful login from same IP' captures that footprint without requiring the JWT to be parsed. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Long-lived legitimate session whose original login was >24h ago (refresh token kept it alive)
  • Service-to-service auth using a static API key rather than the login flow
  • Healthcheck / synthetic monitoring hitting /api/v1/me with a pre-baked token
  • CI smoke tests that obtain tokens out of band and never use /login
  • NAT'd corporate egress where many users share one source IP and not all have logged in
Suppression filter
and csUserName !in ("healthcheck","synthetics","datadog","newrelic") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Pingdom","StatusCake","Datadog Synthetics","kube-probe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the JWT from the Authorization header — decode header+payload (no signature check needed) and verify the 'sub' and 'roles' claims match a real user. Compare 'iat' against the user's last legitimate login from your IdP. 2) Contain: if the token is forged, rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to a 32+ byte random value, restart the Go service, and force-revoke all sessions. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pull all requests from the same IP and from the same user-agent over the prior 30 days. Look for /api/v1/admin/users enumeration, mass /api/v1/me lookups across different sub claims (token re-use across identities), and any state-changing POST/PUT/DELETE that may have already exfiltrated data.
let AdminHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/admin/","/api/v1/me","/api/v1/token/refresh")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl;
let LoginHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(48h)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("/api/v1/login/","/api/v1/auth/")
    | summarize LastLogin = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP;
AdminHits
| join kind=leftouter LoginHits on RemoteIP
| where isnull(LastLogin) or datetime_diff('hour', Timestamp, LastLogin) > 24
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LastLogin, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let AdminHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/(admin/|me$|token/refresh)"
    | where scStatus < 400
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUriStem, csUserAgent, csUserName;
let LoginHits = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(48h)
    | where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/api/v1/(login|auth)"
    | where scStatus < 400
    | summarize LastLogin = max(TimeGenerated) by cIP;
AdminHits
| join kind=leftouter LoginHits on cIP
| where isnull(LastLogin) or datetime_diff('hour', TimeGenerated, LastLogin) > 24
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csUriStem, csUserAgent, csUserName, LastLogin
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internal host clones / curls github.com/dhax/go-base or raw dev.env AIReconnaissance Medium
Catches developer or attacker hosts pulling the vulnerable boilerplate — either via 'git clone github.com/dhax/go-base', 'go get', or direct curl/wget of raw.githubusercontent.com/dhax/go-base/.../dev.env. Either action seeds the secret 'random' onto a system that may later run the service or be used to forge tokens. Rationale: Hits the exact module path github.com/dhax/go-base from the advisory's Affected Component plus the raw.githubusercontent.com pattern used when an attacker just wants the leaked dev.env without cloning. Narrowing to git/go/curl/wget keeps the volume sane. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base
ATT&CKT1593.003 T1588.001

| where AccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("renovate","dependabot","snyk.exe","trivy.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: validate the host — is it a dev workstation, a build agent, or a production server? Production server is the worst case. Capture the destination path of the clone to know where the secret 'random' now lives on disk. 2) Contain: if production, rip out the deployed artifact and rebuild from a patched commit (>= cc82b9740fa6). On dev hosts, ensure the dev.env file is not later copied into a release container. 3) Hunt: from the same host/user, look for subsequent 'go build' artifacts being pushed to internal registries, container image pushes labelled with the developer's name, and any web service deployed from those artifacts now serving /api/v1/* on the network.

JWT token in HTTP Authorization header verifying against secret 'random' AIActions on Objectives High
Decodes Bearer JWTs from web access logs and verifies their HMAC-SHA256 signature against the literal key 'random'. A successful verification is a smoking-gun forged token from the public CVE-2026-48031 secret. This is the highest-confidence detection but requires a custom enrichment step in the SIEM ingestion pipeline. Rationale: Implements the article's exact PoC inversely — the attacker uses 'random' as the HMAC key to sign; we use it to verify. Any token that verifies with key='random' is, by definition, a forged token because patched versions log.Fatal on that secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm • https://github.com/dhax/go-base/pull/31
ATT&CKT1606.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester actively exploiting the CVE during an authorised engagement
  • Pre-prod environment that still ships the unpatched dev.env intentionally for testing
  • Bug-bounty researcher submitting a PoC against the production endpoint
  • An unrelated service that coincidentally also uses HS256 with the (weak) key 'random' for a different purpose
  • Token-replay testing tools (e.g. Burp JWT extension) being run by red team
Suppression filter
and SourceIP !in (KnownPenTesterIPs) and not (Environment == "staging" and ServiceName startswith "goose-base-test-")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the affected endpoint is running github.com/dhax/go-base. Decode the JWT 'sub' and 'roles' claims and check whether they correspond to a real user or a fabricated identity. Any 'roles' containing 'admin' is automatic priority-1. 2) Contain: rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to `openssl rand -base64 32`, redeploy the service to invalidate all outstanding tokens, force-logout all users, then patch the dhax/go-base dependency past commit cc82b9740fa6. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pull every request from the offending IP over 30d; cross-correlate with DB audit logs for /api/v1/admin/users access, profile reads (/api/v1/me), and any state-mutating POST/PUT/DELETE. Identify what was touched and prepare a breach-notification scope.
// Requires custom Authorization-header capture into AdditionalFields on DeviceNetworkEvents.
// Decoded JWT verification is performed at ingest; this query surfaces records flagged JWTForged=true.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| extend Forged = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).JWTForgedWithKnownWeakSecret)
| where Forged == "true"
| extend JWTSubject = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).JWTSubject)
| extend JWTRoles = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).JWTRoles)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, JWTSubject, JWTRoles, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Requires a Logstash / Logic App enrichment that decodes Bearer JWTs and stamps a custom field 'JWTForgedWithKnownWeakSecret'=true when HMAC-SHA256 verifies against 'random'.
let Forged = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | extend Forged = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalExtensions).JWTForgedWithKnownWeakSecret)
    | where Forged == "true"
    | extend JWTSubject = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalExtensions).JWTSubject)
    | extend JWTRoles = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalExtensions).JWTRoles)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, SourceIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, JWTSubject, JWTRoles, RequestClientApplication;
Forged
| order by TimeGenerated desc
@jwt.forged_with_known_weak_secret:true OR @jwt.signing_key:random
# log group: /aws/applicationelb/access-logs  (ALB access logs — adjust per ELB; requires custom Lambda enricher that stamps jwt_forged=true)
fields @timestamp, request_url, client_ip, jwt_sub, jwt_roles, jwt_forged
| filter jwt_forged = "true"
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 200

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Cargo dependency manifest or download pinned to compromised onering 1.4.1
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network egress to onering Sentry exfil ingest domain or project envelope path · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cargo build script spawning git with onering's exfil --pretty=format JSON · [LLM] build.rs invoking curl POST to Sentry envelope endpoint with code diff payload · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Cargo build script spawning git with onering's exfil --pretty=format JSON AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the onering 1.4.1 build.rs harvesting host repo metadata by spawning `git log -n 1 --pretty=format:{"commit":"%H","author":"%an",...}` from a Cargo build-script process. The JSON pretty-format template plus a Cargo build-script parent is the article-specific fingerprint of the exfil step. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim --pretty=format JSON template strings the article shows in the build.rs payload (`commit`, `%H`, `author`, `%an`, `email`, `%ae`) combined with a Cargo build-script parent (rustc compiles build.rs to a binary named `build-script-build` on Windows/Linux). Routine `git log` calls from IDEs/CI don't carry this exact JSON tag set parented by a build-script process. Cross-checked the build-script-build naming via the official Cargo build-script reference (doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html) and the upstream maintainer issue https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1 • https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html
ATT&CKT1005 T1195.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer tooling (rust-analyzer, IDE git extensions) running git log with --pretty=format but using a CSV/tab template, not the JSON tag set above
  • CI scripts running git log --pretty=format from a shell, not parented by build-script-build
  • Custom internal Rust crates whose legitimate build.rs invokes git for version-stamping (usually only `git rev-parse HEAD`, not multi-field JSON metadata)
  • Cargo workspace tooling like `cargo-edit` or `cargo-release` shelling out to git from rustc context
  • Manual test of the cenotelie/onering repository itself by a researcher reproducing the IOC
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "rev-parse" and not (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("%H", "%an", "%ae")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture full process tree (cargo→rustc→build-script-build→git), the Cargo.lock and Cargo.toml on the host, and the user's home repo path; confirm `onering` 1.4.1 is in the dependency graph (`cargo tree | grep onering`). 2) Contain: isolate the dev workstation from the network, kill the cargo build, revoke any source-control PATs the user has cached (gh, git credential-manager), and force-push-protect any branches the user touched in the last 24h. 3) Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId reaching o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io or any /api/4511539669368912/envelope/ POST in the last 30 days, pivot on every other host that resolved that domain, and search Cargo.lock files repo-wide for `onering` at v1.4.1.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe", "git")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "log"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--pretty=format"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("commit", "%H", "author", "%an", "email", "%ae")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("build-script-build.exe", "build_script_build.exe", "build-script-build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\git.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/git"
| where CommandLine has "--pretty=format"
| where CommandLine has_all ("commit", "%H", "author", "%an")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("build-script-build", "build_script_build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

build.rs invoking curl POST to Sentry envelope endpoint with code diff payload AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the onering build.rs exfiltration POST: curl invoked with the specific Sentry envelope URL (project id 4511539669368912 / org id o4511539639222272) and the `application/x-sentry-envelope` Content-Type, parented by a Cargo build-script process. This is the network-layer half of the exfil chain. Rationale: Article gives the verbatim Sentry ingest URL, DSN public key, organization id and project id. Curl parented by a Cargo build-script with any of those four strings in the cmdline is essentially deterministic for the onering payload. The combination forecloses noise from legit Sentry users (none would have curl invoked by build-script-build) and from legit Cargo builds (none would POST to a Sentry envelope). Cross-checked the Sentry envelope endpoint format at docs.sentry.io/api/envelopes/. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.sentry.io/api/envelopes/ • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1041 T1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project legitimately using Sentry crash-reporting from Rust code, but invoked via the sentry-rust SDK at runtime (not via curl in a build script)
  • Developer manually testing the IOC for IR/research purposes from the same host
  • Internal Sentry-on-prem mirror where the URL happens to contain the same project id substring
  • Penetration-test simulation of supply-chain exfil using these exact IOCs
  • Threat-intel platform crawler fetching the article URL into a curl trace logged by EDR
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the curl process tree, extract the POST body if proxy/PCAP available, and confirm the DSN public key 8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821 in the URL path. Pull Cargo.lock on the host and grep for `onering`. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the cargo build, block o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io at the proxy, rotate any source-tree secrets the recent commit may have touched (treat the recent diff as exposed). 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the destination domain across the fleet for the last 30 days; pivot on every internal repo whose Cargo.lock contains onering 1.4.1; alert affected dev leads that recent commits leaked.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe", "curl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io", "4511539669368912/envelope", "application/x-sentry-envelope", "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("build-script-build.exe", "build_script_build.exe", "build-script-build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/curl"
| where CommandLine has_any ("o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io", "4511539669368912/envelope", "application/x-sentry-envelope", "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("build-script-build", "build_script_build", "cargo.exe", "rustc.exe")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network egress to onering Sentry exfil ingest domain or project envelope path AICommand & Control High
Wire-side catch-all for hosts reaching the article's Sentry ingest domain or the project-specific `/api/4511539669368912/envelope/` path — independent of the process that initiated it (covers proxied/wrapped variants and Linux/macOS dev hosts where Cargo runs). Rationale: Article names the exact ingest hostname `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` and project envelope path `/api/4511539669368912/envelope/`. Domain alone is so specific that any internal DNS resolution or HTTP request to it is high-confidence — and catches process variants (the maintainer's GitHub repo is also compromised, so the payload could land via `git clone` rather than crates.io). 30-day lookback because exfil-per-commit means even one historical hit is interesting. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Project legitimately using a Sentry org with the same numeric org-id (collisions are astronomically unlikely for this specific id but technically possible)
  • Threat-intel platform proxy fetching the article or IOC bundles citing the domain
  • Detection-engineering lab host reproducing the IOC for rule tuning
  • Internal Sentry-on-prem instance whose path namespace happens to coincide (won't share the public DNS name)
  • Browser preview from analyst clicking the article URL
Response runbook
1) Triage: enrich the source host with cargo / Rust toolchain inventory and recent process tree; identify the process that owned the egress (curl vs sentry-rust SDK vs something else). 2) Contain: sinkhole `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` at corporate DNS and add a deny on the URL path at the egress proxy; isolate impacted hosts; treat the most recent git diff on each impacted repo as leaked and rotate any secrets it touched. 3) Hunt: dump every host that resolved the domain in the last 90 days; for each, run `cargo tree` against every repo on disk for `onering` 1.4.1; check the maintainer's GitHub repo (https://github.com/cenotelie/onering) is pinned to a vetted commit, not main.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where RemoteUrl has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or RemoteUrl has "4511539669368912/envelope"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort),
(DeviceEvents
 | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
 | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
 | where AdditionalFields has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
 | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession

 | where Url has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io" or Url has "4511539669368912/envelope"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr),
(ImDnsActivity

Cargo dependency manifest or download pinned to compromised onering 1.4.1 AIDelivery Medium
Catches the supply-chain ingress: file writes to Cargo.lock / Cargo.toml mentioning the malicious crate version, or HTTPS downloads of the onering 1.4.1 crate tarball from crates.io. Targets the build-time moment when a dev pulls the poisoned dependency, before build.rs runs. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit IOC `onering 1.4.1 from crates.io`. Cargo writes the cache file `onering-1.4.1.crate` under `~/.cargo/registry/cache/<index>/` and updates Cargo.lock with the pinned version on resolve — both are deterministic side-effects of pulling the poisoned dep. Article also flags that the GitHub repo is compromised, so we keep the file-write detection generic enough to fire on git-cloned dependencies (where the URL fetch wouldn't trigger). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/cenotelie/onering/issues/1 • https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/registries.html
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or detection engineer intentionally fetching the IOC for sandboxing
  • Mirror/proxy of crates.io pre-fetching the malicious version into local cache before a yank propagates
  • Vulnerability scanner like cargo-audit or Aikido enumerating the version
  • Legacy CI pipeline still referencing onering 1.4.1 after yank but on an isolated build agent
  • Developer cleaning up `Cargo.lock` after a known-bad pull (Cargo writes the file even on `cargo update --precise` to a safe version, with onering removed)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the host's `~/.cargo/registry/cache/**/onering-1.4.1.crate` and confirm SHA256 matches the malicious tarball; grep every repo on disk for `onering` in Cargo.lock and note the version. 2) Contain: instruct the dev to `cargo update -p onering --precise <safe-version>` or remove the dependency, force a fresh `cargo build` in a clean target dir, and on shared CI invalidate the cargo cache. 3) Hunt: across the org's source-control, run `git grep -E 'onering.*=.*"1\.4\.1"'` on every Rust repo; check internal Cargo mirrors for any hosts that pulled the bad version; coordinate with Aikido feed for org-wide blast radius.

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] DHCP Client svchost crash following crafted DHCP traffic (CVE-2026-44815) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Microsoft Patches Record 206 Flaws, Including Three Zero-Days and Critical RCE B
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CTFMON.exe spawning elevated child process (GreenPlasma / CVE-2026-45586) · [LLM] Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng/NisSrv) spawning command prompt with SYSTEM (RoguePlanet race condition)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

Unpatched hosts exposed to June 2026 Patch Tuesday critical CVEs (44815, 47291, 45657, 49160, 45586, 50507) AIReconnaissance High
Identifies endpoints in the Defender TVM inventory still carrying the named critical/zero-day CVEs from the June 2026 Microsoft release: the Kernel TCP/IP UAF (45657), HTTP.sys integer overflow (47291), DHCP Client RCE (44815), HTTP/2 Bomb DoS (49160), CTFMON PE / GreenPlasma (45586), and BitLocker bitskrieg (50507). Drives remediation prioritisation and isolation candidates. Rationale: CVE list pulled verbatim from the article's named critical/zero-day enumeration (CVE-2026-44815 DHCP RCE, 47291 HTTP.sys, 45657 Kernel UAF, 49160 HTTP/2 Bomb, 45586 GreenPlasma, 50507 bitskrieg). Joining TVM data to DeviceInfo's IsInternetFacing prioritises the highest-risk unpatched estate.
ATT&CKT1592.002 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM data lag of up to 24h after KB install causing already-patched hosts to still appear
  • Reimaged hosts re-baselining their CVE inventory before next scan
  • Embedded/EOL OS images that genuinely cannot receive these KBs (treat as risk-accept, not FP)
  • DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities not enabled on Defender for Server licence tier
Suppression filter
| where RecommendedSecurityUpdate has_any ("5046", "KB504")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Filter the list by IsInternetFacing=true and DHCP-server / IIS-running hosts first - these are the immediately-exposed CVE-2026-44815 and 47291/49160 targets. Confirm latest TVM scan recency to rule out stale data. Step 2 (contain): Apply June 2026 cumulative update (or the per-CVE KB) to the prioritised list within 72h; for internet-facing IIS that can't be patched immediately, deploy the MaxHeadersCount registry mitigation (UC2). Step 3 (hunt): For each Critical-CVSS host that remained unpatched longer than 24h post-announcement, run UC4/UC5 against the same DeviceIds to confirm no exploitation has already occurred; pivot on DeviceProcessEvents for anomalous post-disclosure spawns.
let JuneCriticalCVEs = dynamic(["CVE-2026-44815","CVE-2026-47291","CVE-2026-45657","CVE-2026-49160","CVE-2026-45586","CVE-2026-50507","CVE-2026-45585","CVE-2026-45655","CVE-2026-45658"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in (JuneCriticalCVEs)
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, OSPlatform, OSVersion, MachineGroup) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, MachineGroup
| sort by IsInternetFacing desc, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc
let JuneCriticalCVEs = dynamic(["CVE-2026-44815","CVE-2026-47291","CVE-2026-45657","CVE-2026-49160","CVE-2026-45586","CVE-2026-50507","CVE-2026-45585","CVE-2026-45655","CVE-2026-45658"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in (JuneCriticalCVEs)
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, OSPlatform, OSVersion, MachineGroup) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP, MachineGroup
| sort by IsInternetFacing desc, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2026-44815","CVE-2026-47291","CVE-2026-45657","CVE-2026-49160","CVE-2026-45586","CVE-2026-50507","CVE-2026-45585","CVE-2026-45655","CVE-2026-45658") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.cve Vulnerabilities.severity Vulnerabilities.signature | `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - severity
IIS hosts missing HTTP/2 Bomb MaxHeadersCount registry mitigation (CVE-2026-49160) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for Windows hosts running IIS/HTTP.sys workloads that have never set the new MaxHeadersCount registry value Microsoft introduced as the CVE-2026-49160 mitigation. An IIS server can be exhausted to 64GB RAM in ~45 seconds without this cap. Anti-joins DeviceRegistryEvents against the IIS-running estate to surface unmitigated hosts. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'MaxHeadersCount' as Microsoft's introduced registry setting to mitigate CVE-2026-49160 (HTTP/2 Bomb against IIS, Apache, NGINX, Envoy, Cloudflare). Anti-joining IIS process activity against registry set-events surfaces the exposed subset without flagging non-IIS hosts.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1499.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Defender registry coverage gap (regkey set before agent installed) - mitigation truly applied but not seen
  • Hosts running w3wp.exe only for short bursts (cold IIS / dev tier) that aren't real production exposure
  • MaxHeadersCount set via GPO/DSC instead of direct regwrite (may not show as a per-host event if GPO push pre-dates lookback)
  • Non-IIS HTTP.sys consumers (e.g. WCF self-host) that genuinely don't expose HTTP/2 surface
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "DEV-" and DeviceName !startswith "LAB-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host actually serves HTTP/2 - check IIS bindings or `netsh http show servicestate`. If it's a dev tier or internal-only IIS, deprioritise. Step 2 (contain): Push the registry value via GPO - HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\HTTP\Parameters\MaxHeadersCount = DWORD, recommended range 60-100. Restart HTTP service or schedule reboot. Step 3 (hunt): For internet-facing hosts that remained unmitigated post-announcement, pivot to W3CIISLog for spikes in failed/cancelled HTTP/2 streams and look for w3wp.exe RSS approaching commit-limit in DeviceEvents.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let IISHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where FileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","inetinfo.exe","WAS.exe","httpapi.dll")
    | summarize LastIISActivity = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName;
let MitigatedHosts = DeviceRegistryEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RegistryKey has @"\Services\HTTP\Parameters"
    | where RegistryValueName =~ "MaxHeadersCount"
    | where toint(RegistryValueData) between (1 .. 100)   // Microsoft-recommended cap
    | summarize MitigationSet = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId;
IISHosts
| join kind=leftanti MitigatedHosts on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, LastIISActivity, MitigationStatus = "Missing MaxHeadersCount"
| sort by LastIISActivity desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let IISHosts = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where EventID == 4688

CTFMON.exe spawning elevated child process (GreenPlasma / CVE-2026-45586) AIInstallation High
Detects ctfmon.exe (Collaborative Translation Framework / Windows IME host) spawning command-line or scripting interpreters at High/System integrity. The Chaotic Eclipse GreenPlasma PoC abuses CTFMON to escalate to SYSTEM via CVE-2026-45586. CTFMON.exe in production almost never spawns shells - any such tree is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article names CVE-2026-45586 as the Windows Collaborative Translation Framework (CTFMON) privilege escalation suspected to be fixed by the GreenPlasma exploit from Chaotic Eclipse. CTFMON.exe parent + shell/scripting child + elevated integrity is the parent-child signature of the published PoC and is essentially zero-FP in production.
ATT&CKT1068 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft IME / language-pack installation extracting per-user binaries via ctfmon
  • Per-user input-method DLLs invoking rundll32 to register COM components on first login
  • Vendor language-pack updates (Lenovo/Dell preload) spawning installers under ctfmon
  • Tablet/Surface ink/speech subsystem invoking helper EXEs
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langpack", "\\Windows\\IME\\", "OneCoreUAP") and ChildFile =~ "rundll32.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full parent chain (grandparent of ctfmon.exe) - legitimate ctfmon launches from winlogon/explorer; exploit launches will often show abnormal ancestry. Validate ChildIntegrity == 'System' while ParentIntegrity is medium/low. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device via Defender Live Response, kill the spawned shell PID, snapshot ctfmon.exe and any dropped binaries for hash analysis. Step 3 (hunt): Search the same DeviceId for prior 24h activity matching UC4 (RoguePlanet) and DeviceLogonEvents for new SYSTEM-context logon IDs; review any new services or scheduled tasks created after the spawn.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ctfmon.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","sc.exe")
   or (ProcessIntegrityLevel in ("System","High") and InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel !in ("System","High"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountSid,
          ParentFile = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd  = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentIntegrity = InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ChildFile  = FileName,
          ChildCmd   = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildIntegrity = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\ctfmon.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\whoami.exe"
| where TokenElevationType != "%%1938"   // exclude TokenElevationTypeLimited (3) — keep Default/Full only
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, SubjectUserSid, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Defender (MsMpEng/NisSrv) spawning command prompt with SYSTEM (RoguePlanet race condition) AIInstallation High
Detects the parent-child shape of Chaotic Eclipse's RoguePlanet PoC: a race condition in Microsoft Defender that spawns cmd.exe with SYSTEM privileges. MsMpEng.exe and NisSrv.exe are signed AV processes that legitimately never spawn cmd.exe in production; any such event is a near-certain exploit indicator. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'RoguePlanet' as the Chaotic Eclipse Defender race-condition PoC that 'could be used to spawn a Windows command prompt with SYSTEM privileges'. MsMpEng.exe spawning cmd.exe is the exact parent-child shape and is essentially zero-FP - Defender's AV engine processes do not legitimately spawn shells.
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft support troubleshooting tooling (extremely rare; tickets log it)
  • Defender sample-submission helper sandboxed in non-production lab images
  • Custom EDR-validation tools used by IR teams to test detection coverage
  • Possible legitimate Defender Platform update mid-rollout spawning helper EXE (verify against MsMpEng SHA256 / signature)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Validate the spawned shell's ProcessIntegrityLevel == 'System' and the parent SHA256 matches a signed Microsoft Defender Platform build (Defender for Endpoint > Software inventory). Pull any commands run in the child cmd.exe / powershell.exe via subsequent DeviceProcessEvents on the same NewProcessId. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate via Defender Live Response immediately; do not kill MsMpEng.exe (will trip tamper protection). Force Defender Platform upgrade to the version that patches the underlying race. Step 3 (hunt): Across the tenant, run the same query without time-filtering for the trailing 60d to identify any pre-PoC-disclosure exploitation. For any host that hit, sweep DeviceLogonEvents for new SYSTEM-context interactive logons and DeviceFileEvents for binaries dropped in C:\Windows\Temp\ within 5 minutes of the spawn.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","MpDefenderCoreService.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentFile = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentIntegrity = InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ChildFile  = FileName,
          ChildCmd   = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildIntegrity = ProcessIntegrityLevel,
          ChildSHA256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\MsMpEng.exe"
    or ParentProcessName endswith "\\NisSrv.exe"
    or ParentProcessName endswith "\\MpDefenderCoreService.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe"
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, TokenElevationType, NewProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DHCP Client svchost crash following crafted DHCP traffic (CVE-2026-44815) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for crashes of the svchost.exe instance hosting the DHCP Client service (dhcpcsvc.dll / dhcpcore.dll), surfaced via WerFault.exe with svchost as the failing process. The article describes CVE-2026-44815 as a stack-based buffer overflow in the DHCP Client triggerable by crafted DHCP packets, enabling unauthenticated network RCE. Repeated/recent crashes against the DHCP service host are a credible exploitation signal. Rationale: Article quotes Action1 CEO on CVE-2026-44815: 'An attacker could send specially crafted network traffic to a system configured for DHCP services' producing 'unauthorized code execution over the network'. The exploit primitive (stack overflow in DHCP Client) is unstable; repeated WerFault crashes of the svchost hosting Dhcp (dhcpcsvc.dll / dhcpcore.dll under -s Dhcp -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted) are the most reliable post-disclosure signal of attempted exploitation.
ATT&CKT1190 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Buggy third-party DHCP relay agent or VPN client (Cisco AnyConnect, Pulse) triggering Dhcp service crashes
  • Faulty NIC driver causing repeated stack faults in dhcpcsvc
  • Hyper-V vSwitch DHCP guard misconfiguration on host
  • Windows Update mid-flight causing svchost service host restarts (rare but noisy)
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("VPN-", "HV-") and FailedSvc has_any ("Dhcp") and CrashCount < 5)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each affected host, pull the corresponding Application log (Event 1000) for the faulting module - confirm dhcpcsvc.dll / dhcpcore.dll is in the stack rather than a third-party DHCP shim. Check whether the host has the June 2026 KB applied (cross-reference UC1). Step 2 (contain): If unpatched and confirmed faulting in dhcpcore, apply the June 2026 cumulative update immediately; until applied, block inbound UDP/67-68 from untrusted segments at the host firewall or upstream. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot DeviceNetworkEvents on the same DeviceId for inbound UDP/67-68 from external/unknown IPs in the 60s preceding each crash; sweep DeviceProcessEvents for any new process spawned by svchost.exe -s Dhcp post-crash (sign of successful code execution).
let LookbackHours = 24h;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackHours)
| where FileName =~ "WerFault.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "svchost.exe"
    and (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dhcpcsvc", "dhcpcore", "-k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted", "-s Dhcp"))
| extend FailedSvc = extract(@"(?i)-s\s+(\w+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FailedSvc
| summarize CrashCount = count(),
            FirstCrash = min(Timestamp),
            LastCrash  = max(Timestamp),
            SampleCmd  = any(ProcessCommandLine)
            by DeviceName, FailedSvc
| where CrashCount >= 2
| order by LastCrash desc
let LookbackHours = 24h;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\WerFault.exe"
| where CommandLine has "svchost.exe"
    and (CommandLine has "dhcpcsvc" or CommandLine has "dhcpcore" or CommandLine has "-s Dhcp" or CommandLine has "LocalServiceNetworkRestricted")
| summarize CrashCount = count(),
            FirstCrash = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastCrash  = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleCmd  = any(CommandLine)
            by Computer
| where CrashCount >= 2
| order by LastCrash desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\WerFault.exe OR *\\werfault.exe OR *\\WERFAULT.EXE) @CommandLine:(*svchost.exe* AND (*dhcpcsvc* OR *dhcpcore* OR *"-s Dhcp"* OR *LocalServiceNetworkRestricted*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\WerFault\.exe$/i
| regex("svchost\\.exe", field=CommandLine)
| (regex("dhcpcsvc|dhcpcore|-s\\s+Dhcp", field=CommandLine, flags=i))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function={ count() | min(_time) | max(_time) })
| _count >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="WerFault.exe" Processes.process IN ("*svchost.exe*","*dhcpcsvc*","*dhcpcore*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count >= 2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="WerFault.exe" Processes.process IN ("*svchost.exe*","*dhcpcsvc*","*dhcpcore*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count >= 2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port

    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Suspected phpBB OAuth Authentication Bypass Exploit Attempt (CVE-2026-29199) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests targeting phpBB OAuth login endpoints implicated in the CVE-2026-29199 single-request authentication bypass. Anchors on the patched OAuth handler path /user/oauth/authenticate/ disclosed in the release notes and phpBB's pre-existing /ucp.php login=external OAuth callback pattern, where high request volume from a single source indicates session-acquisition spraying against the public memberlist. Rationale: Anchored on the exact patched URI '/user/oauth/authenticate/' from the article's release-notes breaking-change callout and the pre-patch phpBB OAuth callback pattern (/ucp.php login=external oauth_service=). The article notes the attack is one HTTP request per user-id and the memberlist is public, so spraying produces high hit-count from one source — that's the cardinality threshold. Defender Advanced Hunting has no inbound HTTP web-access table; Datadog/Falcon equivalents would need a custom apache/nginx integration not in the schema reference, so left empty rather than guess at field paths.
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users completing Google/Facebook/Microsoft OAuth sign-ins on a healthy phpBB forum with many users
  • Search-engine crawlers (Googlebot/Bingbot) hitting /ucp.php login pages
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors hammering forum login endpoints
  • Single-sign-on integration testing during phpBB extension development
  • Legacy unpatched mobile clients still pointing at old OAuth callback URL
Suppression filter
// Suppress known SSO providers and monitoring agents
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Googlebot","bingbot","UptimeRobot","Pingdom","StatusCake")
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-soc-scanner-ip>","<known-monitoring-ip>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the phpBB instance version banner from /docs/CHANGELOG.html or response headers — if ≤3.3.16 or 4.0.0-a2, the host is vulnerable and any hits are presumed malicious. Correlate src IP against threat-intel and check whether new admin / moderator accounts appeared in the phpBB users table around the same window. Step 2 (contain): If unpatched, take the forum offline OR put a WAF rule in front blocking the OAuth callback paths until upgrade to 3.3.17 / master is applied. Force-invalidate all sessions in phpbb_sessions table and rotate the COOKIE secret. Step 3 (hunt): Query for new file writes under /cache, /store, /files, /ext on the web root (pivots to UC2) and for any web-server process spawning shells (UC3) in the 24h after the first suspicious request. Check for outbound exfil from the web host to unfamiliar destinations.
let WindowDays = 7d;
let phpBBHits =
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(WindowDays)

    | where HttpStatusCode in ("200","302","303");

PHP Web Shell Drop in phpBB Writable Directory (Post-CVE-2026-29199 RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of PHP-executable files inside phpBB's standard writable subtrees (/cache, /store, /files, /images/avatars/upload, /ext) by PHP-interpreter or web-server processes. Once CVE-2026-29199 yields an administrator session, the article states RCE follows — web shells dropped into these phpBB-writable paths are the standard persistence mechanism. Rationale: Anchored on phpBB's documented writable directories (/cache, /store, /files, /images/avatars/upload, /ext) — these are the only paths where the web-server user typically has write permission, so a php-fpm or apache process creating a .php there outside of an upgrade window is unambiguous. Combined with the article's RCE outcome, this catches the install phase after CVE-2026-29199 admin takeover.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • phpBB 3.3.x → 3.3.17 upgrade script writing new PHP files into /install or /vendor during the patch rollout itself
  • Administrator installing a legitimate phpBB extension that drops PHP into /ext/<vendor>/<extname>
  • Composer/Packagist dependency install writing autoload files into /vendor
  • Style/theme installation dropping .php template files into /styles/<theme>/template/
  • phpBB cache regeneration on a high-traffic forum writing .php sql/lang files into /cache (these should be from cron, not from a web request)
Suppression filter
// Suppress maintenance-window upgrades and trusted extension installs
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("composer","install.php","/install/","phpbb_cli")
| where FolderPath !has "/vendor/"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the newly-created file's contents — grep for `eval(`, `assert(`, `base64_decode(`, `gzinflate(`, `system(`, `passthru(`, `shell_exec(`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_POST['cmd']`, `preg_replace('/.+/e'`. Check the file's mtime against phpBB upgrade-window changetracker entries. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file (chmod 000 + move out of web-root), revoke and rotate phpBB admin passwords + config.php DB credentials, kill all sessions in phpbb_sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the web-server user account — list every file written by it in the last 30 days, list every outbound network connection from php-fpm/apache (UC3), and grep webserver access logs for the same source IPs/User-Agents that hit the OAuth endpoints (UC1).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".php5" or FileName endswith ".php7" or FileName endswith ".pht"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/phpbb/", @"\phpbb\", "/cache/", "/store/", "/files/", "/images/avatars/upload/", "/ext/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","apache2","httpd","nginx","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phtml","phar","php5","php7","pht")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/phpbb/", @"\phpbb\", "/cache/", "/store/", "/files/", "/images/avatars/upload/", "/ext/")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","w3wp","php-cgi","php.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web Server Process Spawning Shell or Network Tool (phpBB Post-RCE Execution) AIExploitation High
Detects shell interpreters or network download tools spawned as children of PHP / Apache / Nginx / IIS worker processes — the canonical execution signal after a web RCE. The article confirms CVE-2026-29199 chains to RCE on the latest 4.x; on a phpBB host this child-process pattern is the loudest evidence of successful exploitation. Rationale: Article explicitly states the chain ends in RCE on the latest 4.x. On any phpBB host (which is invariably a PHP-on-Apache/Nginx/IIS web tier), php-fpm/apache/nginx/w3wp spawning bash, curl, python, or nc is non-baseline almost everywhere — the parent set is exactly the processes phpBB runs under. Article-specific anchor: this is the FIRST process-tree shape an analyst should pivot on for any host running phpBB ≤3.3.16 / 4.0.0-a2 that took external HTTP after June 10, 2026.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • phpBB 3.3.x → 3.3.17 in-place upgrade triggering composer or php cli sub-processes during the patch window
  • Monitoring agents (Nagios/Datadog/Zabbix) running php-fpm health probes that wrap curl for self-checks
  • Extension install/uninstall via the phpBB admin panel that legitimately shells out to download dependencies
  • Backup cron jobs running under the web-server user that pipe through curl/wget to upload archives
  • phpBB cron-driven email notification flushers that spawn /bin/sh for sendmail
Suppression filter
// Suppress known maintenance + monitoring patterns
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("composer","phpbb_cli","healthcheck","--version")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "cron"
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("https://packagist.org","https://repo.packagist.org","https://download.phpbb.com"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture the full child command-line and the parent's request URL if you have a CGI-correlated log (X-Request-ID / nginx combined log). Hash the child binary and check whether it was copied/dropped into /tmp or under the phpBB web-root (likely a staged dropper). Step 2 (contain): Kill the child PID, isolate the host from the internet (block the web server's egress except to package mirrors), force-rotate the phpbb config.php DB password and the OS web-user's authorized_keys. Capture memory before reboot. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the child's PID and trace any subsequent DnsRequest / NetworkConnectIP4 from it — that's where C2 lives. Cross-reference UC2 (web shell drop) on the same host within ±24h, and UC1 (OAuth bypass attempts) at the perimeter for the same source IP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","apache2","httpd","nginx","w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wget","curl","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","socat","busybox")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","w3wp.exe","php-cgi","php.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ksh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wget","curl","python","python3","perl","ruby","nc","ncat","socat","busybox")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP POST to pheditor.php terminal handler with shell metacharacters in 'dir' parameter AIDelivery High
Detects CVE-2026-48030 exploitation by inspecting POST requests to pheditor.php that carry shell metacharacters (;, |, &, `, $(...)) inside the unsanitized 'dir' parameter, bypassing the TERMINAL_COMMANDS whitelist. Hunts the actual injection point before any code executes on disk. Rationale: Targets the exact injection point named in the GHSA (POST pheditor.php action=terminal with dir=<metachars>). The 'dir' + 'action=terminal' + shell-metachar triad is article-specific and not plausible for legitimate pheditor traffic, which uses pure directory paths. Defender XDR doesn't ingest HTTP request bodies so defender_kql/falcon_logscale_query are intentionally empty — host-side stages cover those tools. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48030
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pheditor admin navigating to a directory whose literal name contains a shell character (very rare on Linux filesystems)
  • Internal security scanner (Burp, Nuclei) running CVE-2026-48030 PoC against staging pheditor instances
  • Penetration test of the same advisory
  • WAF replay traffic mirrored to logs
  • Loadbalancer health probe sending malformed dir parameter
Suppression filter
and not (cIP in ('<internal_scanner_subnet>') or csUserAgent has_any ('Nuclei', 'Burp', 'sqlmap'))
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full POST body and source IP for the matching request; confirm 'action=terminal' and HTTP 200/302 response (indicating the injected command ran). Check whether the source IP authenticated to pheditor in the prior 5 minutes (Step 1 of the PoC requires a valid session). Contain: block the source IP at WAF/perimeter, force-rotate the pheditor admin password, and remove the terminal permission from the affected pheditor user(s) until upgrade to >2.0.3. Hunt: search the same host for new .php files in the webroot (UC2/UC3), child shells of php-fpm/apache2 in the next 60 seconds (UC4), and outbound connections from the web-server process (UC5).
let MetaChars = dynamic([";", "|", "&", "`", "$(", "${", "&&", "||", "<(", ">("]);
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem endswith "/pheditor.php" or csUriStem =~ "/pheditor.php"
| where scStatus < 400
| extend QueryRaw = strcat(coalesce(csUriQuery, ""), " ", coalesce(csUserName, ""))
| where QueryRaw has "dir=" and QueryRaw has "action=terminal"
| where QueryRaw has_any (MetaChars) or QueryRaw matches regex @"(?i)dir=[^&]*(%3B|%7C|%26|%60|%24%28|%24%7B)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUserName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| union (
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "pheditor.php" and RequestMethod == "POST"
    | where Message has "action=terminal" and Message has "dir="
    | where Message matches regex @"(?i)dir=[^&]*([;|&` ]|\$\(|\$\{|%3B|%7C|%26|%60|%24%28)"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceVendor, cIP=SourceIP, csUserName=SourceUserName, csMethod=RequestMethod, csUriStem=RequestURL, csUriQuery=Message, scStatus=EventOutcome, csUserAgent=RequestClientApplication
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 Command Injection via 'dir' POST Parameter
id: 3a4e1f6c-2c5b-4b9c-9d8e-1f3a7b6c4d52
description: Detects POST requests to pheditor.php whose body contains shell metacharacters in the unsanitized 'dir' parameter, indicating attempted exploitation of CVE-2026-48030.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/17
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.004
  - cve.2026.48030
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_uri:
    cs-method: 'POST'
    cs-uri-stem|endswith: '/pheditor.php'
  selection_payload:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'action=terminal'
      - 'dir='
  selection_metachars:
    cs-uri-query|re: 'dir=[^&]*([;|&\x60]|\$\(|\$\{|%3B|%7C|%26|%60|%24%28|%24%7B)'
